body_markdown:
*Welcome to our monthly market report, where we sum up the previous month’s activity in the collector car market with charts and key talking points using the data we gather every day.*


## Key Takeaways


- The[Hagerty Market Rating](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/how-the-hagerty-market-rating-works/) , which measures the status of the collector car market in terms of activity or “heat,” dropped about a tenth of a point from the previous month to 58.63. Again, the change was minimal, as it has been for much of the year despite frenzied activity in smaller pockets of the market. (The Market Rating measures the market as a whole, and any rating between 50 and 60 is still considered “flat market” territory.)
- $1M+ lots are up 79% year-over-year in count (540 vs. 302) and now account for 30% of global dollar volume, up from 21% a year ago. That share is essentially flat compared to September (31%), so the trophy-segment concentration has stopped expanding for now.
- Online activity in the $1M+ segment continues to increase, as 15 million-dollar lots sold online, the most of any month this year (the previous high was 14 in May). Live events still dominate this segment, though, as 45 million-dollar lots sold at live auctions in October alone, and 443 of the 540 total $1M+ lots (82%) through October have gone through a live auction, not an online one.
- Ferrari is responsible for roughly 45% of the year-to-date global auction sales increase, identical to its September share.
- Modern cars keep growing in importance. Vehicles from 1990 and later represent 55% of lots offered year to date (up from 53% a year ago), but 59% of dollar volume (up from 51% in 2025). Price appreciation is driving the shift of the latter.
- Premium cars are still setting the pace, but the broader live auction market cooled a bit this month. The growth in October came almost entirely from higher prices, not more cars changing hands​
